lead: This unit turns the qubit into a working object: postulates, superposition, Bloch sphere, measurement, composite states and entanglement. By the end you can compute measurement probabilities, trace out a subsystem, write Bell states and evaluate a CHSH game.
about: The unit starts with the four postulates (2.1) and the bit–qubit comparison (2.2). Chapter 2.3 builds superposition, and 2.4 maps pure qubit states to the Bloch sphere. Measurement (2.5) then explains probabilities and collapse. Composite systems (2.6) introduce density matrices and the reduced state. Entanglement and Bell states (2.7) follow, leading to Bell's inequality and the CHSH game (2.8). The final chapter (2.9) ties measurement to the Stern-Gerlach experiment and the uncertainty principle. Each chapter uses the same qubit examples, so the mathematics stays connected.

chapters.idea: Four postulates link quantum states, unitary evolution, measurement and composite systems.
chapters.depth: Cover the four postulates: a state is a unit vector in Hilbert space; closed-system evolution is unitary; measurement is projective with the Born rule; composite systems use tensor products. State the density-operator form only as a pointer. Some syllabi call this 'basic postulates' or 'postulates of quantum mechanics and operator algebra'.

figure.title: Four postulates
figure.aria: A central postulates box branches to state, evolution, measurement and composite system, numbered one to four.

chapters.example: A qubit is in |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩. (a) Check normalisation. (b) Find the probability of outcome 0 and outcome 1 in the computational basis. (c) Apply X = [[0,1],[1,0]] and write the new state. Answer: (a) (√3/2)² + (1/2)² = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. (b) p(0)=3/4, p(1)=1/4. (c) X|ψ⟩ = (1/2)|0⟩ + (√3/2)|1⟩.
chapters.trap: Squaring the amplitude instead of taking its modulus squared, and forgetting that postulate 3 renormalises the state after measurement.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Hilbert spaces, Dirac notation, unitary matrices.
chapters.leave: Density operators to 2.6; gate details to Unit 3; algorithms to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A classical bit is 0 or 1; a qubit is a unit vector with complex amplitudes and returns one bit on measurement.
chapters.depth: Define a classical bit as a choice between 0 and 1. Define a qubit as |ψ⟩=α|0⟩+β|1⟩ with |α|²+|β|²=1. Explain that global phase has no physical effect and that measurement returns one classical bit. Point to interference as the source of quantum advantage; algorithms are Unit 4. Some syllabi call this 'quantum bits' or 'representations of qubits'.

figure.title: Bit versus qubit
figure.aria: A progression from a classical bit to a qubit state, then measurement probabilities, then one classical result.

chapters.example: A qubit has α = 1/√2 and β = i/√2. (a) Check normalisation. (b) Find p(0) and p(1). (c) If the outcome is 0, write the state after measurement. Answer: (a) |1/√2|² + |i/√2|² = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. (b) p(0)=1/2, p(1)=1/2. (c) |0⟩.
chapters.trap: Saying a qubit is 'both 0 and 1 at the same time' and forgetting that one measurement gives only one bit; also treating global phase as observable.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1; Unit 1: complex numbers and Dirac notation.
chapters.leave: Single-qubit gates to Unit 3; Bloch sphere to 2.4.

chapters.idea: Superposition is a linear combination of basis states with complex amplitudes, and relative phase controls interference.
chapters.depth: Explain superposition as a linear combination in a chosen basis. Show |+⟩ and |−⟩, relative phase, and interference after a second gate. Use H as the standard example. Some syllabi call this 'superposition principle'.

figure.aria: A box tree expands a qubit state into two basis branches with amplitudes alpha and beta.

chapters.example: Start in |0⟩. (a) Apply H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] and write the state. (b) Find p(0) and p(1). (c) Apply Z = diag(1,−1) to the result and show the probabilities are unchanged. Answer: (a) H|0⟩ = (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 = |+⟩. (b) p(0)=p(1)=1/2. (c) Z|+⟩ = (|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 = |−⟩, still p(0)=p(1)=1/2.
chapters.trap: Dropping relative phase because it does not show in computational-basis probabilities; it changes results after later gates.

chapters.idea: Any pure qubit state maps to a point on the unit Bloch sphere with polar angle θ and azimuth φ.
chapters.depth: Derive |ψ⟩=cos(θ/2)|0⟩+e^{iφ}sin(θ/2)|1⟩ with θ∈[0,π], φ∈[0,2π). Mark poles and equator states. Explain that Pauli gates rotate the Bloch vector and that mixed states lie inside. Some syllabi call this 'Bloch sphere representation of a qubit'.

figure.aria: A schematic Bloch sphere with north and south poles, four equator states, and dashed axes.

chapters.example: A pure qubit state is |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩. (a) Find θ and φ. (b) Write the Bloch vector. Answer: (a) cos(θ/2)=√3/2 gives θ/2=π/6, so θ=π/3; sin(θ/2)=1/2 and the coefficient 1/2 is positive real, so φ=0. (b) (sinθ cosφ, sinθ sinφ, cosθ) = (√3/2, 0, 1/2).
chapters.trap: Using θ instead of θ/2 in the amplitudes, and thinking a global phase moves the point on the sphere.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2.2–2.3; Unit 1: trigonometry and complex numbers.
chapters.leave: Mixed states to 2.6; gate rotations to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Measurement is projective, probabilistic and changes the state according to the Born rule.
chapters.depth: Give the Born rule for projective measurement: p(m)=⟨ψ|P_m|ψ⟩, state after outcome m is P_m|ψ⟩/√p_m. Work in computational and rotated bases. Mention POVMs as general measurements; only a few universities teach POVM details here. Some syllabi call this 'measurement in quantum mechanical system'.

figure.title: Projective measurement
figure.aria: A state passes through a projector to give an outcome and a renormalised collapsed state.

chapters.example: Measure |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩ in the {|+⟩,|−⟩} basis. (a) Find p(+) and p(−). (b) Give the state after each outcome. Answer: ⟨+|ψ⟩=(√3+1)/(2√2), so p(+)=(2+√3)/4≈0.933; p(−)=(2−√3)/4≈0.067. After +: |+⟩; after −: |−⟩.
chapters.trap: Using the amplitude, not its modulus squared, for probability; and forgetting to renormalise the collapsed state.
chapters.leave: POVM details and open systems to advanced courses; uncertainty to 2.9.

chapters.idea: Composite systems live in tensor-product spaces; tracing out one part gives a reduced density matrix, which can be mixed.
chapters.depth: Define density operator ρ=Σ p_i|ψ_i⟩⟨ψ_i|, pure vs mixed, tr ρ=1, ρ²=ρ for pure. Define tensor-product composite states. Define partial trace and reduced state ρ_A=tr_B ρ_AB. Some syllabi call this 'density operators' and 'composite systems'.

figure.title: Reduced state
figure.aria: A pure composite state becomes a density matrix, then tracing out B leaves the reduced state of A.

chapters.example: Let |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2. (a) Write ρ_AB. (b) Trace out B and find ρ_A. (c) Show ρ_A is mixed. Answer: ρ_AB=|Φ+⟩⟨Φ+|. ρ_A=tr_B ρ_AB = (1/2)(|0⟩⟨0|+|1⟩⟨1|)=I/2. tr ρ_A²=1/2<1, so mixed.
chapters.trap: Writing a ket for the reduced state of an entangled pair; a reduced state can be mixed and needs a density matrix.
chapters.leave: Entanglement tests to 2.7–2.8; quantum channels to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Entangled states cannot be factored into product states, and Bell states are the standard two-qubit examples.
chapters.depth: Define entanglement as non-factorability. List the four Bell states with normalisation. Explain the EPR argument and no-signalling. Mention no-cloning only as a one-line consequence; full proof is in Unit 3. Some syllabi call this 'Bell states' and 'EPR paradox'.

figure.title: EPR pair
figure.aria: An EPR source sends one qubit to Alice and one to Bob, and their measured bits meet at a comparison block.

chapters.example: Show that |Φ+⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 is entangled by trying |Φ+⟩=(a|0⟩+b|1⟩)⊗(c|0⟩+d|1⟩). Then measure the first qubit in the computational basis. Give the joint probabilities and Bob's state for each Alice outcome. Answer: ac=1/√2, bd=1/√2, ad=0, bc=0; no complex numbers a,b,c,d satisfy all four, so entangled. Outcomes: p(00)=p(11)=1/2. If Alice gets 0, Bob has |0⟩; if Alice gets 1, Bob has |1⟩.
chapters.trap: Thinking entanglement sends a signal faster than light; local outcomes are random and only correlations show after comparison.
chapters.leave: Teleportation and no-cloning proof to Unit 3; Bell tests to 2.8.

chapters.idea: Local hidden variables obey CHSH ≤ 2, while quantum mechanics reaches 2√2 and wins the CHSH game more often than classical physics.
chapters.depth: Write CHSH as S=⟨A_0B_0⟩+⟨A_0B_1⟩+⟨A_1B_0⟩−⟨A_1B_1⟩. Classical local hidden variables give |S|≤2; quantum mechanics gives |S|≤2√2. In the CHSH game classical win probability is 3/4; the Bell state strategy gives cos²(π/8)≈0.8536. Some syllabi call this 'Bell inequality violation experiments' and 'CHSH'.

figure.aria: A sequence diagram of the CHSH game: referee sends bits x and y to Alice and Bob, who return outputs a and b.

chapters.example: In the CHSH game Alice and Bob share |Φ+⟩. For input x=0 Alice measures Z; for x=1 she measures X. For y=0 Bob measures (Z+X)/√2; for y=1 he measures (Z−X)/√2. For x=0, y=0, find the probability that a=b. Answer: the correlation is ⟨Z⊗(Z+X)/√2⟩ = 1/√2. So P(a=b)=(1+1/√2)/2=(2+√2)/4≈0.8536. The other three input pairs give the same value by symmetry.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the CHSH value bound (2 vs 2√2) with the game win probability (3/4 vs 0.8536), and treating the quantum strategy as signalling.
chapters.leave: Loophole-free experiments to advanced reading; QKD to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Stern-Gerlach shows quantised spin and measurement disturbance, while the uncertainty principle limits simultaneous sharpness of incompatible observables.
chapters.depth: Describe the Stern-Gerlach experiment with silver atoms and an inhomogeneous magnetic field. Explain sequential magnets along z and x, quantised spin, and measurement disturbance. State the Robertson uncertainty relation ΔA ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩| and apply it to S_x, S_y. Some syllabi call this 'Stern-Gerlach experiment' and 'uncertainty principle'.

figure.title: Stern-Gerlach
figure.aria: Silver atoms pass an inhomogeneous magnet and split into two spin beams on a screen.

chapters.example: A silver atom beam passes a Stern-Gerlach magnet along z. (a) What fraction exits each z port? (b) The upper z beam enters an x-oriented magnet. What fraction of the original beam exits each x port? (c) For a spin state with ΔS_x=ħ/2 and ⟨S_z⟩=ħ/2, find the minimum ΔS_y. Answer: (a) 1/2 and 1/2. (b) 1/4 and 1/4 of the original beam. (c) [S_x,S_y]=iħS_z, so ΔS_x ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩|. Thus (ħ/2)ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)(ħ/2), giving ΔS_y ≥ ħ/2.
chapters.trap: Adding probabilities along different SG axes (should be 1/2 each, not 1) and treating the uncertainty relation as a statement about clumsy instruments rather than intrinsic spread.
chapters.leave: Spin matrices and Pauli algebra to Unit 3; detailed atomic physics out of scope.
